text: Longitudinal and cross-sectional blood coagulation studies were conducted in patients receiving oral contraceptive therapy and in unmedicated women serving as control subjects. These studies involved the use of a novel technique called plasma fibrinogen chromatography, which, through an assay for high-molecular-weight fibrinogen complexes in plasma, can detect or exclude the presence of small thrombi, including those that may not be clinically apparent. A new class of contraceptives, specifically Ovulen containing 100 pg of mestranol and Demulen containing 50 pg of ethinyl estradiol, was administered to participants over a period of one year. Participants were monitored longitudinally for up to ten years during the cross-sectional study, where serial examinations were performed on those using oral contraceptives for three to ten years. Overall, pathologic plasma fibrinogen chromatographic findings indicated the development of thrombotic lesions in 6 percent of control examinations and 27 percent of samples from oral contraceptive users. This suggests that oral contraceptive users had a higher incidence of clinically silent thrombotic events compared to controls, indicating a four-to-fivefold increased risk of developing clinically overt diseases. Therefore, it is inferred that they are at a significantly elevated risk of developing such conditions, aligning with the risk factors identified through epidemiological studies.
